🇨🇦 Trade talks between the U.S. and Canada fell apart late last night, and both sides said steep new tariffs will go into effect. It's an unprecedented breakdown in relations with the second-largest U.S. trading partner, Axios' Ben Berkowitz and Courtenay Brown report.

🪖 Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is expected to head to the private sector in the coming months after tension with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, The Wall Street Journal scoops.
 
 
1 big thing — Scoop: Rogers-AIPAC rupture roils Michigan Senate race
 

Mike Rogers. Photo illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Photo: Sarah Rice/Getty Images
 

Allies of former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, Michigan's GOP nominee for the U.S. Senate, have asked AIPAC not to advertise on his behalf, triggering a rupture with the powerful but polarizing pro-Israel group, Axios' Alex Isenstadt reports.

  • Rogers spoke with AIPAC chair Michael Tuchin in Los Angeles last week. The next day, AIPAC shelved an already-cut video ad targeting Rogers' Democratic rival, outspoken Israel critic Abdul El-Sayed.

Why it matters: The extraordinary tension underscores how far AIPAC's political standing has fallen amid voters' anger over the war in Gaza.

  • Even Rogers — a staunchly pro-Israel Republican — fears the group's public support could be a liability in the Nov. 3 election.

⚡ Driving the news: The move by Rogers' team angered AIPAC officials, who had spent more than $30 million to try to defeat El-Sayed in the Democratic primary and prepared to spend millions more to help elect Rogers, according to people familiar with the conversations.

Zoom out: El-Sayed made AIPAC a centerpiece of his successful primary campaign, using the group's spending against him to portray Democratic opponent Haley Stevens as beholden to the pro-Israel lobby.

  • El-Sayed has called Israel a "rogue state," accused it of genocide and apartheid, and has declined to say whether Israel has a right to exist as a Jewish state.
  • That made defeating him a priority for AIPAC, which rarely mounts major spending campaigns in general elections.

👀 Behind the scenes: Rogers' team warned AIPAC before the Aug. 4 Democratic primary that it believed El-Sayed would beat Stevens, though AIPAC held out hope Stevens would prevail. The two sides agreed to keep talking.

  • After El-Sayed narrowly won, AIPAC told Rogers' allies it wanted to continue its advertising offensive into the Nov. 3 general election.
  • But Rogers' team believed AIPAC's primary ads had backfired by giving El-Sayed a powerful foil — one he was eager to use again.
  • "AIPAC, if you're listening, come back and burn it again," El-Sayed said before his primary victory.

Rogers' allies urged AIPAC to get involved without putting the group's name front and center, people familiar with the talks told Axios.

  • One option: Directing AIPAC donors to a pro-Rogers super PAC instead of the group running its own ads, or a joint fundraising group the Rogers campaign has established with the national GOP.
  • Rogers' team also proposed hiring AIPAC's political strategists to help guide its effort.
  • But AIPAC officials weren't satisfied: The group wanted a visible role in defeating El-Sayed and argued that because Rogers is strongly pro-Israel, El-Sayed would tie him to the pro-Israel lobbying group regardless.

🔎 State of play: Direct talks between Rogers' team and AIPAC have now gone cold, prompting a broader GOP effort to broker peace. Jewish Republican donors with ties to both sides are acting as intermediaries, people familiar with the discussions said.

  • Some national Republicans now worry that AIPAC — whose super PAC ended July with nearly $60 million in the bank — will sit out the general election entirely.

"I welcome any and all support from the pro-Israel community, and I'm proud to have their involvement," Rogers told Axios.

  • AIPAC representatives didn't respond to requests for comment.

2. ⛽ Midterms vs. markets
 

President Trump. Photo illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Photo: Alex Grimm/Getty Images
 

President Trump is reaching deeper into individual markets to try to bring down consumer prices.

  • Why it matters: The administration is under mounting pressure to deliver relief as affordability becomes a bigger political liability ahead of the midterms, Axios' Courtenay Brown writes.

The moves:

  • 🥩 Beef: Trump said yesterday that he will temporarily waive tariffs on up to 300,000 metric tons of additional beef imports for 90 days, a period that would last through the midterms.
  • 💰 Borrowing costs: The administration has tried to push down longer-term rates through Treasury debt purchases and moves to lower mortgage rates. This week's initial relief was short-lived.
  • ⛽ Gas: Trump has pushed energy companies to cut pump prices as the Iran war sent oil prices soaring.
  • 🛍️ Retail: The White House has pressed major retailers to cut prices, touting recent reductions by Walmart and others.

The other side: Prescription drugs are a bright spot, with prices dropping at the quickest rate in six decades due to a mix of Trump- and Biden-era policies, as well as market forces.

3. ✨ Wall Street's AI blind spot
 

Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios
 

There's a growing disconnect between the business and politics of data centers, Axios' Dan Primack writes.

  • The business is booming. Public and private equities are both up and to the right — not only for actual project operators, but also for related energy and vendor plays.
  • The politics have turned sharply negative, often on a bipartisan basis. A growing number of states have implemented or are considering moratoriums and bans.

🪧 Behind the scenes: Data center investors lament the opposition, often framing it as a correctable community education issue. They also believe that much of the political pushback will dissipate after the midterm elections.

  • But Wall Street and Silicon Valley aren't the electorate. "We can't let China win the AI race" isn't a salient statement for most normies, particularly when their electricity bills keep rising.

A Wall Street executive active in the sector told us: "There is a time horizon problem. ... Capital is underwriting decades of demand while politics runs to the next election. Those two things at times don't reconcile easily."

4. 💃 Ballroom back on
 
Marine One, carrying President Trump, flies over construction on the new White House ballroom yesterday. Photo: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

The Supreme Court ruled yesterday that President Trump's sprawling ballroom project can proceed for now, despite a lower court's ruling that halted the administration's plans.

  • In a brief order, Chief Justice John Roberts paused the D.C. District Court's restrictions on construction while the court weighs the administration's request. The order didn't address the project's legality or give a timeline for when SCOTUS will weigh in, Axios' Avery Lotz and Josephine Walker write.
President Trump and first lady Melania Trump arrive for an event announcing the expansion of a foster care initiative in the Rose Garden of the White House on Thursday. Photo: Finn Gomez/Getty Images

The big picture: The White House has pointed to the alleged plot against the White House's July UFC fight and the White House Correspondents' Dinner attack as evidence of a heightened threat environment that boosts the need for the ballroom and the renovation of a secure bunker below it.

  • A White House official wrote in a filing sent to the Supreme Court that the project is already 65% complete and that construction of the underground facilities is nearly finished.

Zoom out: The joint cost of the ballroom and underground bunker is projected to be at least $600 million, up $400 million from when the project was first announced.

5. 🐊 Florida Dems clash
 
Angie Nixon campaigning this week at Ebenezer Missionary Baptist Church in Hallandale Beach, Fla. Photo: Joe Raedle/Getty Images

Angie Nixon, Florida's new Democratic Senate nominee, and the state party's chair had a heated conversation yesterday that included a yelling match about the impact of socialism and the challenges of campaigning in a red state like Florida, three people familiar with the conversation tell Axios' Holly Otterbein, Marc Caputo and Andrew Pantazi.

  • Why it matters: The conflict exposes the fault line in the party between the progressive base embodied by Nixon and the establishment represented by the state party's chair, Nikki Fried.

🗳️ Zoom in: Nixon, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, who won the primary in a shocking upset over Alex Vindman earlier this week, expressed frustrations to Fried that she had not received sufficient help from the state party.

  • Fried, in return, warned that Nixon's ties to the DSA could give an opening to the GOP to attack her, sources told us.

According to two people who spoke with Nixon, both she and Fried yelled at each other during the call. Another person who spoke to Fried said the chair did not yell but was yelled at.

  • "Nikki wants her to back away from DSA, from socialism," said one person who spoke with Nixon. "She's listening to other people saying that they're afraid, they're scared — the Jewish members and the Hispanic caucus. But to Angie, Nikki doesn't want Angie to be who Angie is. Angie has already done the backing-away."

📞 On the call, Nixon told Fried, "You never gave a care about me from the beginning, and now you're telling me how to run my campaign?" according to the source.

  • At one point, the source said, Nixon yelled, "Stop gaslighting me!"

6. 💼 CEOs' AI dance
 

Illustration: Eniola Odetunde/Axios
 

Simon Hernandez-Arthur — the new author of Axios Communicators, our weekly newsletter covering the biggest trends in the comms industry — writes:

CEOs used to talk up AI progress and efficiency by the number of workers it could replace.

  • Now, with economic angst rising, they're being more careful about linking AI to job cuts.

🤖 Case in point: In 2024, Klarna said its AI assistant was doing the work of 700 full-time agents.

  • Last year, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff said AI helped reduce support headcount from 9,000 to about 5,000 "because I need less heads."

🔎 Now, leaders are wording their statements carefully to distinguish between "AI is reshaping how we work" and "AI is replacing workers."

  • Etsy CEO Kruti Patel Goyal said this month's 220 job cuts "weren't driven by AI," while acknowledging the technology is changing the skills and capabilities Etsy needs.
  • Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman said the 4,800 roles eliminated last month were "not being replaced by AI," while adding that AI is changing how work gets done.

7. 🎓 South's student surge
 
Data: National Center for Education Statistics. Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Visuals

America's future college pipeline is growing in the South and shrinking elsewhere, Axios' Russell Contreras reports.

  • By 2041, the number of high school graduates is projected to fall by 29% in California, 27% in New York and 32% in Illinois, per the Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education.
  • The South's high school graduate population is projected to grow 3%.

8. 🧶 1 for the road: Cash for crafting
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios
 

Americans of all ages are spending more than ever on offline hobbies and crafts, and are increasingly willing to cut elsewhere or dip into their savings, Bloomberg reports ($).

  • Sofia Szyfer, a 25-year-old New York publicist, told Bloomberg she's spending almost $300 every month on stickers, paper goods and craft-related events. She's a devotee of "junk journaling" — a mix of scrapbooking, collage and diary-keeping.
  • Szyfer has cut back on other forms of entertainment: "I'd rather just go and spend $50 on stickers than go to a live event or a live concert."
